title: In his words

posts.hook: No one cheers for you keeping the loan you already have.

cards.text:
No one cheers for you keeping the loan you already have.

Nobody posts about the refinance they didn’t do, the car they didn’t finance, the offset they didn’t touch.

The reason so few people end up with real equity is that the boring decisions never look impressive in the moment, only at the end.

posts.linkedin:
No one cheers for you keeping the loan you already have.

Nobody posts about the refinance they didn’t do, the car they didn’t finance, the offset they didn’t touch. There’s no before-and-after photo for leaving a good loan alone.

But that’s most of what building equity actually looks like from the inside. Pay lands in the offset. Spare cash stays there. The loan you were tempted to move for a tiny saving stays put. Year one feels like nothing. Year five looks like luck to everyone else.

The boring decisions never look impressive in the moment. Only at the end.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: The bank will tell you the most you can borrow.

cards.text:
The bank will tell you the most you can borrow.

Nobody tells you the most you can comfortably repay.

Those are different numbers. We quote the second one first, because approval and affordability are not the same thing, and living at the edge of what a lender will give you rarely buys a better life.

posts.linkedin:
The bank will tell you the most you can borrow.

Nobody tells you the most you can comfortably repay. Those are different numbers, and most people only ever hear the first one.

When we quote borrowing capacity we give the comfortable figure first. Could we squeeze more if we pushed? Usually. But approval and affordability are not the same thing, and living at the very edge of what a lender will give you rarely buys a better life.

So you get two numbers from us: the one you can hold through a couple of rate moves, and the stretch. Plan on the first. Keep the second in the drawer.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Everyone compares rates. Almost nobody compares structures.

cards.text:
Everyone compares rates. Almost nobody compares structures.

A rate changes every few months. A structure decides what you can do for the next ten years.

If all you want is a sharper rate, call your bank. We’re here for how the loan is built.

posts.linkedin:
Everyone compares rates. Almost nobody compares structures.

A rate changes every few months. Banks are competitive on it, and one call to your lender’s retention team usually fixes a rate problem. You don’t need us for that.

A structure is different. How the debt is split, what’s secured against what, where the offsets sit, whether the setup still works for the next thing you want to do. Those decisions compound for a decade, and nobody at a branch is paid to think about them.

So before you refinance, ask one question: is this a rate problem or a structure problem?

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Interest on your investment loan is usually deductible.

cards.text:
Interest on your investment loan is usually deductible.

Interest on the home you live in isn’t.

So every spare dollar has a better home. It’s just not the one most people send it to. Worth a conversation with your accountant.

posts.linkedin:
Interest on your investment loan is usually deductible. Interest on the home you live in isn’t.

So every spare dollar has a better home, and it’s usually not the one people send it to. Paying down the investment loan feels responsible. It also shrinks a deduction. Paying down your own home loan cuts interest you can never claim.

Our general view: keep investment debt interest-only, point repayments and the offset at the home loan, and revisit if you ever plan to move into the investment.

The tax side depends on your situation, so have your accountant in that conversation.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Redraw feels like savings. It isn’t.

cards.text:
Redraw feels like savings. It isn’t.

It’s money you’ve already paid off your home loan. Pull it out for an investment and you’ve muddied what that loan was for.

A separate split for the investment keeps the story clean. Your accountant will thank you later.

posts.linkedin:
Redraw feels like savings. It isn’t.

It’s money you’ve already paid off your home loan. The moment you pull it back out to fund an investment, you’ve mixed two purposes in one loan, and the purpose is what decides what you can claim.

The cleaner approach is to reduce the home loan limit and set up a separate split for the investment. Same money, different label, a story your accountant can actually follow in three years’ time.

It takes a bit of planning and some cost up front. Untangling it later costs more.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Buying your first home? The loan is the easy bit.

cards.text:
Buying your first home? The loan is the easy bit.

The hard part is knowing whether the place is good value, what to offer, when to walk, and what the contract actually says.

You do the inspecting. We do the data, the digging and the negotiation, all the way to the keys.

posts.linkedin:
Buying your first home? The loan is the easy bit.

Finance is the part everyone worries about and, with the right preparation, the part that goes fastest. The hard part is everything around it: working out if a place is actually good value, spotting a body corporate problem before it’s yours, knowing what to offer and when to walk, and keeping the contract and settlement on track.

That’s where we spend most of our time with first-home buyers. You do the inspecting, because how a place feels when you walk in matters most. We do the data, the due diligence and the negotiation alongside you, all the way to the keys.

posts.hook: The bank said no. That’s one bank.

cards.text:
The bank said no.

That’s one bank. One credit team, one policy, one way of reading your payslips.

It isn’t the answer. Half the files we end up settling were a no somewhere else first, because the income was real but the story was told badly.

posts.linkedin:
The bank said no. That’s one bank.

One credit team, one policy, one way of reading your payslips. It isn’t the answer, it’s an answer.

A surprising number of the files we settle were a no somewhere else first. Self-employed income read as unstable. Shift penalties ignored. A probation period treated as a risk instead of a start date. The income was real; the story was told badly, or told to the wrong desk.

If you’ve been knocked back, the useful question isn’t “what’s wrong with me”. It’s “who reads this kind of income properly, and how do we present it”.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Sign for thirty years. Pay it off in twenty-five anyway.

cards.text:
Sign for thirty years. Pay it off in twenty-five anyway.

The longer term sets a lower minimum repayment, and the minimum is what every lender uses to work out what else you can borrow.

What’s on paper and what you actually do can be two different things.

posts.linkedin:
Sign for thirty years. Pay it off in twenty-five anyway.

Clients refinancing often ask to keep the loan at twenty-five years to match the old one. The instinct is good: don’t stretch the debt out. We’d still write it over thirty.

The longer term sets a lower minimum repayment, and the minimum repayment is what every lender uses when they work out what else you can borrow. That protects your capacity for the next purchase.

The actual paying down is done by you: higher repayments you set yourself, and an offset you keep building. Same finish line, with room to move if life changes.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: The buyer’s agent says buy first. The selling agent says sell first.

cards.text:
The buyer’s agent says buy first.

The selling agent says sell first.

Both are good at their jobs. Both are also describing the order that pays them. Run the numbers with someone who gets paid the same either way, then let the agents do what they’re good at.

posts.linkedin:
The buyer’s agent says buy first. The selling agent says sell first.

Both can be good at their jobs and still give advice shaped by their own timeline and fee. That isn’t cynicism, it’s just how incentives work.

So when you’re upgrading, we ask clients to isolate that advice for a moment. Run the buy-first and sell-first numbers with someone who gets paid the same either way. Decide on your finances. Then brief the agents on the plan and let them do what they’re genuinely good at.

Ask who gets paid when you take their advice. It’s not rude. It’s due diligence.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: A bigger deposit feels safer. A buffer usually is.

cards.text:
A bigger deposit feels safer. A buffer usually is.

If you qualify for a low-deposit scheme, we often prefer using it and keeping part of your savings back in an offset.

A slightly bigger loan with money behind you beats a smaller loan and an empty account.

posts.linkedin:
A bigger deposit feels safer. A buffer usually is.

First-home buyers who qualify for a low-deposit scheme often want to tip every dollar into the deposit anyway, because a smaller loan feels like the responsible move. We usually suggest the opposite: use the scheme, keep part of the savings back, park it in an offset.

Yes, you borrow a bit more, so you need the capacity for it. But the money in the offset saves interest exactly as if you’d paid it in, and it’s still yours when the hot water system dies in month three.

A slightly bigger loan with money behind you beats a smaller loan and an empty account.

General information only, not personal advice.

posts.hook: Five boring money decisions that quietly build equity.

cards.text:
Five boring money decisions that quietly build equity.

None of them will impress anyone at a barbecue.

All of them show up on your loan balance in five years.

Your pay lands in the offset, not a savings account.

Savings interest gets taxed. Offset interest saved doesn’t.

Same money, one of them is working harder for you.

Upsizing? Keep cash back for the first two or three years.

A slightly smaller deposit and a healthy offset beats tipping everything in.

The buffer is there while you get used to the bigger repayment.

Don’t ask how much buffer you have.

Ask how many months it buys.

A lump sum is just anxiety. A number of months is a plan with a review date.

Most people buy a car within six months of buying a home.

Plan it before the loan settles, not after it has eaten your budget.

The mortgage was never the thing that made the repayments tight.

posts.linkedin:
Five boring money decisions that quietly build equity.

None of them will impress anyone at a barbecue. All of them show up on your loan balance in five years.

Your pay lands in the offset, not a savings account. Savings interest gets taxed; offset interest saved doesn’t.

If you’re upsizing, keep cash back for the first few years rather than tipping it all into the deposit.

Measure your buffer in months, not dollars. A lump sum is anxiety; a number of months is a plan.

And plan the car. Most people buy one within six months of settling, and it’s the car loan, not the mortgage, that makes the budget tight.

General information only, not personal advice.

Pay into the offset. Keep a buffer when you upsize. Count that buffer in months, not dollars. Plan the car before it plans you. None of it is exciting. All of it compounds.

Which of the five is the one you’ve been putting off?

posts.hook: What a broker actually does, in five lines.

cards.text:
What a broker actually does, in five lines.

Not the version on the website.

The version that explains why some clients stay for fifteen years.

You don’t pay us. The bank does, and every bank pays about the same.

So we don’t have a favourite.

The only thing that moves our recommendation is your file.

We ask every bank before we tell them who you are.

Then we apply once.

One application on your file, to the lender that already said yes in principle.

If your broker only talked about rate, you got a transaction, not advice.

Rates change every few months.

Structure is the thing that decides what you can do next.

Settlement isn’t the end. It’s where our job starts again.

Rate reviews, an equity check, a call when something in your life changes.

That’s the part nobody puts on the website either.

posts.hook: Buying an investment with your home’s equity? Five lines on getting the structure right.

cards.text:
Buying an investment with your home’s equity?

The loan you get is easy. The structure you get is what matters.

Five lines we keep coming back to.

Keep the two properties in separate lanes.

The deposit comes from its own split against your home. Nothing is tied to anything else.

Separate security is what keeps you flexible later.

Equity sitting in an offset costs you nothing until you use it.

Set the facility up now, park it, and the repayment is effectively zero.

You move when the right property turns up, not when the bank is ready.

Investment debt stays interest-only. Your repayments go at the home loan.

One of those interest bills is usually deductible. One never is.

Your accountant should be in this conversation.

Transact through the offset. Never through redraw.

And set up today’s loan for the property after this one.

Restructuring later costs money. Structuring now costs a conversation.

posts.linkedin:
Buying an investment with your home’s equity? The loan is easy. The structure is what matters.

Keep the two properties in separate lanes: the deposit comes from its own split against your home, with nothing tied to anything else.

Park released equity in an offset. Until you use it, it costs you nothing, and you move when the right property turns up.

Keep the investment debt interest-only and aim your repayments at the home loan. One interest bill is usually deductible; one never is. Your accountant should be in that conversation.

Transact through the offset, never through redraw. And set up today’s loan with the next purchase already in mind.

posts.hook: First home, honestly. Five things we tell every buyer.

cards.text:
First home, honestly.

Five things we tell every buyer in the first meeting.

Some of them are not what you want to hear.

Most people can afford the repayments. They can’t afford the deposit.

So we spend our time on deposit pathways, not on telling you to wait for twenty percent.

Prices rarely wait for you.

Roughly five times your income is where borrowing power starts.

Then debts come off it, and different banks give different answers.

It’s a budget to search with, not a number to offer on.

For a first home, a buyer’s agent is rarely worth the fee.

How a place feels when you walk in matters most, and you can do that part.

We’ll do the data, the digging and the negotiation.

The loan is the easy bit.

Value, offer, contract, settlement. That’s where buyers get hurt, and that’s where we spend our time.

You pick the home. We handle the rest.

posts.hook: Refinancing, honestly. Five things a broker doesn’t usually say out loud.

cards.text:
Refinancing, honestly.

Five things a broker doesn’t usually say out loud.

We’d rather you heard them before you signed anything.

We won’t move a loan just to move it.

If you already have a good rate and the switch adds nothing structural, we’ll tell you to stay.

Fees and hassle usually eat a marginal gain.

Your current bank can often do what you need.

A top-up, a variation, a reprice. We ask them first.

Moving is the last option, not the first.

Your rate will move. Your discount shouldn’t.

What we negotiate is the margin below the standard rate, and it stays for the life of the loan.

Ask what discount is written into your contract.

The rate on the proposal is where the haggling starts, not ends.

We keep going back to the pricing desk until settlement.

And switching banks is mostly one form: where your pay goes.
